newsitem.title: GERMANY: POLL-Buba seen skipping policy move chance Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Buba seen skipping policy move chance Tuesday.

text.p: Speculation the Bundesbank would choose Tuesday's securities repurchase tender to signal a change in monetary policy has died under the weight of the strong mark and faltering share markets, a survey showed.

All eight economists surveyed by Reuters on Monday said they expected the central bank to announce a three percent, fixed rate securities repurchase agreement, or repo, continuing a policy dating back to August 1996.
"The dollar is exactly where the Bundesbank wants it," said Gernot Nerb, economist at Salomon Brothers. "There is no need to raise rates now."

Speculation in financial markets the Bundesbank would raise interest rates spread rapidly in recent weeks as the dollar pushed toward 1.90 marks and central bank officials dropped hints they were worried about inflation.
The strong dollar, economists said, raises the prospect of "imported inflation" where more marks are required to buy foreign products such as oil products that are often denominated in dollars.

But with the German currency having clawed its way back to 1.8150 marks, such fears are receding, allowing the Bundesbank to bide its time on monetary policy and consider more fundamental factors like consumer demand and capacity utilisation.
"Now that the dollar has corrected, the Bundesbank is no longer under any time pressure," said Timo Klein, economist at MMS International.
Although there was no clear agreement on the issue, some economists also said weakness on world share markets would also give the German central bank reason to pause.
"Stock market weakness is keeping central banks from making a move on rates, the Bundesbank included," said Craig Shute, economist at Bear Stearns.
Others, however, argued the central bank would not mind seeing share markets fall due to fear that further gains would eventually lead to a correction that could damage the economy.

Although some economists said they expected the Bundesbank to leave rates on hold for the rest of the year, most believed the central bank would tighten monetary policy within the next couple of months.

Economists said that over that time, the domestic economy may finally show signs of life and with German interest rates at historically low levels, the central bank could not waste any time in tightening credit.

Indeed, several said so-called "hawks" on the Bundesbank's policy-making council were already tempted to raise interest rates and that only time was needed to win over "doves" who do not want upset economic recovery with higher rates.
"Time is working in the favour of the hawks," said Joerg Kraemer, economist at Merrill Lynch.
Economists were also divided on what form any future shift in monetary policy might take.

Some thought the Bundesbank would adopt a variable rate repo, allowing market forces to determine the interest rate level. A variable rate, they argued, would enable the central bank to blame market forces if rates ticked up, thus masking its true monetary intentions.
Others saw the Bundesbank maintaining the fixed repo at a higher level, maybe near 3.2 percent.
